sources.title: Kitaro Nishida (Q45125), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): label 'Kitarō Nishida', description 'Japanese philosopher (1870-1945)', born 1870-05-19, died 1945-06-07, citizenship Japan, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nishida Kitaro' by Yoshinori Takeuchi (Kyoto University), read in full: Japanese philosopher whose maiden work Zen no kenkyu (An Inquiry into the Good, 1911) grew from his Zen practice and lectures, who attempted to bring Western philosophy into the Oriental spiritual tradition (the page's AI-generated summary box, not relied on, calls the book the first major work of its kind); Confucian schooling and a lifelong friendship with D. T. Suzuki; Zen practice during his years as a school teacher and professor (diary remarks on Zen 'overwhelmingly conspicuous'); professorship at Kyoto Imperial University 1913/14-1928; the philosophy of the place (topos) of Nothingness; seven volumes of Philosophical Essays after retirement; inspired the Kyoto school; and his critics (nationalists and militarists during the war, later Marxist and anti-metaphysical philosophers, and the philosophically more important criticisms of Takahashi Satomi and Tanabe Hajime). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Written by a Kyoto-school philosopher, so sympathetic in tone.

John C. Maraldo, 'Nishida Kitaro', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (substantive revision 2024), read in full (biography, methods, Asian sources, critiques and influence sections): schooling and Zen practice under Kyoto masters while teaching; drafting An Inquiry into the Good from 1905 and obtaining the Kyoto chair on that basis; reworking Neo-Kantians, Royce, Bergson, Lotze and Husserl; helping bring Tanabe Hajime, Watsuji Tetsuro and Kuki Shuzo to Kyoto and attracting students such as Nishitani, Miki and Tosaka; writing in 'spirals' that revisit earlier formulations; taking critics seriously (Takahashi on pure experience, Soda on place, Tanabe and Tosaka on history) and changing course; persevering with his work during illness and wartime bombing, finishing 'The Logic of Place and the Religious Worldview' two months before his death; the Kyoto School's later influence; and the critique that his system leaves little room for gaps. A scholarly reference entry; the author calls Nishida best considered an independent thinker. His political writings are noted but not scored here.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'NISHIDA Kitaro', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures, read in full: philosopher, graduated from the Imperial University of Tokyo in 1894, taught philosophy and ethics at Kyoto, Zen no Kenkyu (An Inquiry into the Good) described as conceived as the first Japanese philosophical book with creativity, retired 1928, Order of Culture 1940, and his collected works published from 1947 became best-sellers; the site states that all its images are in the public domain. Institutional summary; no behavioural detail.

Kyoto Journal (published by the Kyoto City Tourism Association), 'The Philosopher's Path: Nishida Kitaro's Contemplative Route' (2015), read in full: draws on his biographer Michiko Yusa's Zen and Philosophy (2002) and on his student Nishitani Keiji's memoir; says he began a daily walk in 1910 that he kept until his 1928 retirement, usually alone and for two hours or more; was a wide reader who devoured thinkers' biographies and followed the latest science; found comfort in calligraphy and waka; and, per Nishitani, usually arrived thirty minutes late for special lectures, mumbled for a while and then paced and spoke with intensity, oblivious to his gestures. Also remarks he was drawn into wartime nationalist politics (not scored) and was slow to be recognised abroad. A travel-magazine essay quoting a biographer and a devoted pupil, so partly admiring and secondhand.

Gereon Kopf, review of Michiko Yusa, 'Zen and Philosophy: An Intellectual Biography of Nishida Kitaro', Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 30/1-2 (2003), read in full from the Nanzan Institute PDF: a specialist review of the first comprehensive English-language biography; says it draws on his letters, diaries and notes, corrects errors in the dating of correspondence, presents him as a man of integrity driven by an existential-spiritual quest, notes that his philosophical development was tied to his life, that Yusa writes descriptively but admits being under the 'spell of the Nishidan mystique', and that she tends to adopt Nishida's own interpretation of events. A scholarly secondary source with a critical remark on the biography itself.

Damian Flanagan, review of Keiji Nishitani, 'Nishida Kitaro: The Man and His Thought', The Japan Times (23 February 2019), read in full: a short newspaper review of a pupil's tribute collection; calls Nishida arguably the most important modern Japanese philosopher, says the essays show him turning to Zen in his youth, reading widely, and pursuing a unifying principle of existence he called pure experience in the face of psychology and sociology encroaching on philosophy. Brief and admiring; its remarks on his family life are not used.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_nishida_britannica, src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_ndl, src_nishida_kopf | 1905-1930s | reference biography + encyclopedia entry + national library + biography review] Britannica describes An Inquiry into the Good (1911) as his maiden work, an attempt to merge Western philosophy with Zen and Confucian values, the Library describes it as conceived as the first Japanese philosophical book with creativity, and Britannica and the encyclopedia entry trace his later concepts of the place of Nothingness and the historical body; Kopf's review calls him arguably the most creative philosopher of Japan in the twentieth century. Originality is documented by independent institutional summaries, but it is a judgement about an output rather than a specific creative episode, and critics attacked the metaphysics, so strong inference at moderate confidence.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_britannica | 1911-1945 | encyclopedia entry + reference biography] The encyclopedia entry describes his aim of a comprehensive 'system of self-awareness', his methods of taking the more inclusive as the more concrete, of wholes that reflect themselves in their parts and of returning oppositions to an undifferentiated ground, and Britannica says he extended his philosophy of Nothingness to explain 'historical reality in the historical world'; the entry also notes that critics ask whether such a system can acknowledge gaps. Building and extending an all-encompassing conceptual structure is well documented by two independent reference works, though both are written by sympathetic specialists and describe the system rather than a moment of decision. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): systems_abstraction lowered from 76 / 0.66 to 72 / 0.58 because two reference sources carry the row and the Kopf review notes the biography adopts his own reading.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_britannica, src_nishida_kyotojournal | 1890s-1945 | encyclopedia entry + reference biography + magazine essay] The encyclopedia entry lists his reworking of the Neo-Kantians, Royce, Bergson, Lotze and Husserl, topics from art and morality to history and nationhood, and a pervasive use of Chinese, Indian and Zen sources; Britannica adds Greek philosophy and a mathematics background; the magazine essay says he devoured thinkers' biographies and followed the latest science. Breadth across philosophy, religion, mathematics-trained reasoning and East Asian classics is documented, but it is largely a breadth within philosophy and religion, hence moderate.

persistence.rationale: [src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_britannica | 1905-1945 | encyclopedia entry + reference biography] The encyclopedia entry says that despite failing health and the bombing of cities around him he persisted in his investigations and completed 'The Logic of Place and the Religious Worldview' two months before his death; it and Britannica record that he began composing An Inquiry into the Good in 1905 while teaching, kept up formal Zen practice, and after retirement in 1928 went on writing the seven volumes of Philosophical Essays. A sustained forty-year programme of work is documented, but the two sources are not independent in kind and say little about obstacles other than illness and war. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): persistence lowered from 72 / 0.62 to 68 / 0.56 because two reference sources and no documented episode of overcoming resistance beyond output.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_britannica | 1911-1930s | encyclopedia entry + reference biography] The encyclopedia entry gives specific instances: Takahashi Satomi's criticism of pure experience led him to clarify it in a follow-up article, Soda Kiichiro's criticism of the first formulation of place led him to remove Neo-Kantian comparisons, and Tanabe Hajime's and Tosaka Jun's criticism of his focus on consciousness led him to develop the historical world and historical body; Britannica independently confirms that Takahashi and Tanabe were his most important critics. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70/0.60 because the instances of changing course rest on a single reference entry; Britannica confirms the criticisms but not his responses.

discipline.rationale: [src_nishida_kyotojournal, src_nishida_britannica, src_nishida_sep | 1899-1928 | magazine essay + reference biography + encyclopedia entry] The magazine essay, citing his biographer, says he kept a near-daily walk from 1910 until retirement in 1928; Britannica says he was much engaged in Zen meditation while teaching at Yamaguchi and Kanazawa, with Zen remarks overwhelmingly conspicuous in his diary of the period; the encyclopedia entry says that during the next decade he was more intent on formal meditation practice under Zen masters than on writing essays. A long-running self-imposed routine is documented across three sources, but the same essay reports that he usually arrived about thirty minutes late to special lectures, so the pattern is about private practice rather than punctuality.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_nishida_sep, src_nishida_kyotojournal | 1900s-1940s | encyclopedia entry + magazine essay] The encyclopedia entry says his calligraphy and poetry were renowned in their own right, and the magazine essay says he found comfort in calligraphy and in writing waka; the Kyoto Journal essay also places his daily walks among temples and pines. Two sources agree that he practised and was known for traditional arts, but neither describes specific works or their reception, so the row stays at moderate confidence.

portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (alt-dependent) (lead) / CONFIRMED via the alternative path: the NDL Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures entry for Nishida exists and matches (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/6069/, two photographs, 6069_1.jpg 938x1363 and 6069_2.jpg 1098x1593 downloaded directly from the NDL site). The lead's Commons uploader copies (Earthbound1960) were NOT used. HOLDER RECORD CHECKED: the NDL entry page itself and its 'About This Site' page (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/about/), which states in the 'Reproduction of the contents' section that all images in the exhibition are in the public domain and may be reproduced or reused, including commercially, without application to the NDL, with the source to be cited as 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/)'. The holder does NOT name a photographer or a date for either image, so creator and date are recorded as unknown/undated; the second image shows him in later life in kimono and round spectacles and was chosen because the first carries red stamp marks. No holder contradiction was found; the weakness is the missing photographer attribution, accepted because the holder itself makes an explicit public-domain statement for the whole exhibition (Roster63 precedent for NDL Portraits). The portrait was downscaled only (1098x1593 to 827x1200), never enlarged.

CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nishida Kitaro' https://www.britannica.com/biography/Nishida-Kitaro (read in full; supplemented by the Stanford Encyclopedia entry and the NDL biographical summary).
ATTRIBUTION SCREEN: attributable (lead) / CONFIRMED: attribution_confirmed true. Nishida is a modern figure with surviving diaries, letters, lectures and a scholarly biography; the sources attribute specific practices (Zen training, daily walk, lectures, responses to named critics) to him individually.
SOURCES READ (6 substantive): Britannica (Takeuchi), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Maraldo), NDL Portraits entry, Kyoto Journal essay (Yusa and Nishitani quoted), Kopf's JJRS review of Yusa's biography, Japan Times review of Nishitani's tribute; Wikidata orientation only. PERSPECTIVES: reference biography by a Kyoto-school philosopher; independent encyclopedia entry; national library; a magazine essay quoting a biographer and a pupil; a scholarly review that criticises the biography's reliance on Nishida's own account; a newspaper review. Non-self behavioural sources: Kyoto Journal, Kopf, SEP, Britannica. COUNTER-VOICES: critiques by nationalists, Marxists, anti-metaphysical rationalists, Takahashi Satomi and Tanabe Hajime (Britannica and SEP); the SEP remark that his system leaves little room for acknowledging gaps; Kopf's remark that the biography adopts Nishida's own reading. All secondary accounts derive in part from his diaries and from pupils' memories, so confidence stays <= 0.66 and no score exceeds 76.
NOT OPENED: Nishida's own works (self-report), Yusa's full biography, Nishitani's full memoir (only the passages quoted by Kyoto Journal and the Japan Times), Heisig's Philosophers of Nothingness, Wikipedia, the Nishida Kitaro Museum of Philosophy (site not reachable); the Japan Times reviewer's remarks on his family and temper were not used (private life and unsourced characterisation). Excluded: wartime politics, family bereavements, health.
